caption:
Where did the Stonehenge stones come from? Two very different places.

The big sarsens — 30 uprights, around 26 tons each — came from West Woods in Wiltshire, about 16 miles away. A 2020 study led by David Nash matched 50 of 52 megaliths chemically to that one spot.

The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire, Wales — roughly 150 miles (240 km) away. In 2019 archaeologists found evidence of Megalithic quarrying at the Welsh sources, meaning human hands moved them, not glaciers.

Then it got stranger. At Waun Mawn in Preseli, Mike Parker Pearson's team found a dismantled stone circle 110 m across — exactly the diameter of Stonehenge's first circle — including a stone hole with a pentagonal cross-section matching a Stonehenge bluestone "like a key in a lock". Soil dating put its erection at 3400–3200 BC and its removal 300–400 years later. Human activity there stopped at the same time.

And the Altar Stone came from further still. In 2024 a Curtin University team chemically matched it to the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland — some 430 miles away.

Why carry stones that far? Researchers at the Royal College of Art found the bluestones ring like bells when struck. In the Preseli village of Maenclochog, local bluestones were used as church bells until the 18th century.

What is still open: nobody knows whether the stones went straight from quarry to Salisbury Plain, or whether a whole sacred circle was taken down and rebuilt. The builders left no writing.

Images: Lucas de Heere's watercolour of about 1573–75; Philip Henry Sharpe's 1906 photograph from a Royal Engineers tethered balloon; a 1920 newspaper photograph of restoration work; modern views by Mavratti and by Airman 1st Class Madeline Herzog. All public domain.
